newsitem.title: USA: Away on business: A new airport toy.
newsitem.headline: Away on business: A new airport toy.

text.p: Business travelers with time to kill at the airport may soon have a useful toy: fingertip Internet access at a cost not much different from a long-distance call.
GTE Corp. began testing the concept this summer at the Dallas-Fort Worth airport and says it has caught on so well that negotiatons or preliminary discussions are under way with a number of airports.
The access points called "cyberbooths" are bound to become commonplace "without question," said William Kula, a GTE spokesman in Irving, Texas.
The devices are set up in kiosks and contain keyboards and video screens.

"You don't need a password to log on," said Kula. "The main screen has a start and a help button. You're two clicks away from the World Wide Web. There's a selection box on the second screen that can get you America Online and Compuserve.
"You can retrieve mail from about 90 percent of all E-mail systems that exist today," he added.
Internet access is via the widely used Netscape Navigator 2.01.

In the Texas test the terminals have been available free of charge. When the kiosks become standard, users will have to pay by swiping a credit card through a slot in order to log on. Kula said no fees have been announced "but we anticipate pricing around $5 for 10 to 15 minutes."

The system uses a Gateway 2000 computer with finger-pad mouse. It is armed with Cyber Patrol software, which prevents users from accessing sexually graphic material that might offend passers-by in busy public places.
Kula said research indicates that only one in three business travelers carries a laptop on the road. The kiosks are designed to keep those without a portable computer in touch.
The system would also be of value to someone with a laptop who wants to go on line without unpacking the device and finding a user-friendly telephone.
As configured in the current test, the kiosks contain two Internet access points and two separate sophisticated pay telephone terminals to facilitate laptop use.
The 10 terminals in the test at Dallas-Fort Worth airport have won usage "beyond expectations. Each station per day averages 50 log-ons and each user spends about 12 minutes," Kula said.
"The response has been very favourable," he added, noting that sending and receiving E-mail is the most frequent activity, followed by browsing the World Wide Web.

Based on user reaction from the tests, GTE and the firm that designed the kiosks, San Diego-based Atcom/Info, are planning some enhancements, such as places to store briefcases or luggage while using the kiosks and ways to make the screens The concept may find its way into other settings, such as hotels and shopping centres. Kula said an insallation has just been announced for the the Ala Moana shopping mall in Hawaii and discussions are also under way with the Honolulu airport.
